25 years, that's how long I've been playing Diablo. The Butcher in D1 was the first adrenaline rush a game ever gave me, at age 9. I skipped school to go to a cyber cafe for Diablo 2, got into a fight with my parents for overstaying to finish a dungeon, spent hours on GameFAQs researching builds when I couldn't get back to the cafe. I took a full week of annual leave when Diablo 3 launched.

I bought Diablo 4 at full price on launch because I believed I was buying a game I'd play for years. I was wrong, and not because the game got stale. Because Blizzard deliberately made it worse for people who don't pay more.

With the Lord of Hatred expansion, Blizzard overhauled the entire loot system. Normal and magic items now drop in higher tiers (Torment 1 and 2), and players are expected to use the Horadric Cube to upgrade them. The Horadric Cube is locked behind the Lord of Hatred paywall.

This is categorically different from how Vessel of Hatred handled its paywalled content. Runes were locked behind that expansion too, but runes were supplemental. They weren't a core mechanic the base game was redesigned around. They didn't even appear for players who hadn't bought the DLC. The Horadric Cube is different. The base game's loot loop has been rebuilt with the expectation that you have it. Without it, you're playing a broken version of a game you already paid full price for.

This is planned obsolescence by definition. Blizzard holds an oligopoly in the ARPG space, and they know that long-term fans, the people most emotionally invested in the franchise, are also the least likely to walk away. They're banking on brand loyalty functioning like an addiction. Loyal customers aren't being rewarded. They're being exploited.

The defenders of this will tell you to just buy the expansion, that complaining makes you a 'broke boy,' that the gameplay is great so what's the problem. That's not a rebuttal. That's what it looks like when someone's identity is so wrapped up in a brand that they'll defend the company's right to exploit them. Good visuals and fun combat don't make predatory business practices okay.

After 25 years, I'm done. Just uninstalled. Not because the game isn't fun, it is. But because I refuse to reward a company that views my loyalty as leverage to extract more money from me. There are other ARPGs made by developers who still respect the people who built their franchise.

Legacy Review Pre-Season 4:
Diablo 4 didn't respect my time so I'll keep this short and sum up the main points to decide if this is the game for you:

I got 100% in the game. This is truly a bells and whistles mobile game with as bare game play as is required to reel consumers in. Events are just color changes for enemies/regions, everything else is 100% identical. Aside from the end-game boss loot targeting, there still isn't anything else as mentioned.

- Fun, basic gameplay, with a boring gameplay loop that lacks dopamine hits.
*Each class has 4 builds which can be mix and matched.
*Sacred Ancestral Unique gear only matches some builds.
*Corpses have a small max limit for 2023, damaging two specific builds.
*Forgetful, throwaway music, but is good nonetheless and gets the job 'done.'
*Gameplay feels over a decade behind the times, lacks innovation.
*Inscribing items is the exact same function as the Horadric Cube.
*Enchanting items is 5 steps backwards in this game. You can't see what you can change on the affix until you've spent your material and you can't refund them if you choose no affix.
*All Armor Sets (Green) were removed and sold in the Shop (with no bonus).
*All cool armor & weapon effects from epic sets in past games or even Path of Exile, $. Not a single one for free. Not one.
*Archon, Boneweave, and Sovereign armor sets are 99% identical, most sets look pretty similar as well to goad you into the shop.
*Game freezes on occasion when loading near other players (when streaming them in).

- Feels like the game was made by people who don't play video games.
*Always something to do, but always lacking dopamine hits, i.e., the loot is only ever incrementally good except when first accessing a new world difficulty tier.
*Altars of Lilith can be completely ignored unless min/maxing as the upgrades give mathematical negative returns almost immediately, regardless of the level scaling.
*Mining Ores and doing Herbalism (you just click the deposit/herb, then pick up the item) is required to upgrade Gear and Potions, respectively.
*PvP is both Optional (open mouse wheel -> scroll right -> apply Blood Mark) even in the 2 PvP areas and broken due to a flat '92% damage reduction buff,' which means if you did 5,000 damage now you do 400 (8 x 5000) / 100 , so you still kill someone in 1-3 seconds depending on your class and theirs.
*PvP marked for blood (enables pvp) can glitch out, preventing you from attacking others but enabling them to attack you (when the glitch occurs, you will not have the particle effect so you won't even know). When glitched you must logout to remove the mark.
*PvP is markedly unfinished and poorly thought out, you can reduce pvp damage further by 30% for 20 seconds, but this requires cutting your screen in half with your inventory, then clicking on a tiny box (all mid-battle most likely), then right clicking on a scroll.
*PvP is unbalanced for every class and every build, each fight lasting a second, maybe two.
*I enjoyed the 'Open World' aspect. From a 3D Designer point of view, it isn't really open world, they simply took 5 Acts of areas and stitched them together, removing the loading screen and mostly hand-crafting the over-world. When taken in this way, the world map isn't really that big, and we loved this, even if it creates a lack of cohesion for the player from a world building perspective (i.e., you can cross Estuar in minutes).
*Minus copy paste 'special' bosses to climb the season chapters (which I didn't finish), you have Helltides (Tier 3/4) for targeting loot, Obols (all tiers/from events) for targeting loot, and Nightmare Dungeons (Tier 3/4) for upgrading Paragon board sigils (same function as upgrading gems at the end of a D3 Greater Rift).
*Season and in-game content builds on Diablo Immortal, for better or worse, i.e., to complete the Season 2 content, you have to climb to Tier 3 at the least.
*The loot you get is the same everywhere, nothing has a specific loot table, minus first time kill rewards, for example, Echo of Lilith.
*Tired, boring, cliched, copy-paste story line, trying to be something it's not. Loved Lilith, hated the plot existing to move me from A to B.
*Hitting enemies lacks responsive feedback, they just jitter slightly, flash white/silver, or fight right through it.
*Sounds of hitting enemies with the physical weapons is lackluster.
*Boring, copy paste Affixes for gear.
*Great side quests; Horrible voice acting outside the Main Quest. Shameful, especially horrendous as I played Baldur's Gate 3 for 181 hours before this game so it stuck out like a sore thumb.

- Store front with skins priced at $38.41 CAD after tax for 1 cosmetic armor set.
*Horse armor selling for $23.14 after tax, and WE ALL complained about Bethesda, hah!
*Prices normalized by American Companies & Consumers, pressured and forced onto everyone else due to how the global currency exchange works and has functioned for generations; some companies eat this exchange to increase spending in lower GDP countries, see Fatshark with Warhammer 40,000: Darktide, which eats roughly 56% of the conversion rate for the consumer, and this is but one alternative method of targeted pricing as there are many profitable ways to go about this.
*No 'Statistics' based research has been used (mathematically even if less than 0.1% buy macrotransactions from Diablo 4's store, they make Real Profit), no transparency between professionals and corporations, every game with MTX stores share the same pricing, same scheme, except D4's store lacks 'FOMO' or, Fear of Missing Out, i.e., the shop lacks items and will rotate every item every 24 hours, some into the same slot, some down to the bottom, some up to the recommended. If you feel inclined to buy, just wait, you will never lose out and they never remove items from the shop.
*Game that has soft-lock issues where not enough enemies spawn carrying Animus on occasion.
*Waiting in queue indefinitely, soft-locking in queue, login soft-lock.
*Item windows and comparison windows constantly flash on occasion (appear and disappear) with no apparent fix or cause.
*Enemies die standing up and their model doesn't disappear. Haven't seen any T-posing, they just die with their idle animation active until you log out. Happens frequently in the Blood Harvest seasonal event.

Diablo 4 has a genuinely phenomenal core. 
The moment to moment gameplay is extremely fluid, the combat feels satisfying, and the overall class identity is incredibly well realized. On a technical level, the game is brilliantly optimized for PC with a completely stable frame rate and graphics that scale gracefully across both high end and low end systems. The art direction, the story, and the presentation are top tier. If this game were judged solely on its core mechanics and audiovisual execution, it would easily be a 10 out of 10 masterpiece.

The real problem is the rotten corporate shell surrounding this beautiful core. Every major decision feels designed to farm the player for engagement metrics. They constantly nerf item drops, remove target farming options, and implement absurd XP grinds for the paragon level 300 cap and seasonal war plans. To make matters worse, these war plans are not account wide. Your alternate characters have to start the grind entirely from zero. Even the seasons are artificially short at just three months compared to the five or six months seen in other ARPGs, simply to cycle battle passes and themed cosmetic shops faster. At the end of the day, they use a fantastic game to hook you, only to trap you in a tedious hamster wheel that strips away quality of life to keep corporate numbers high. 

This negative review comes from a place of genuine disappointment because it feels awful when a game stops trying to entertain you and starts trying to exploit you.

I honestly don't know what's wrong with Blizzard anymore, or what the Diablo 4 team has been smoking. But it's definitely nothing good.

Season 13 was actually okay. They improved a lot of things and finally seemed to be heading in the right direction. Even though the system around Kanai's Cube still feels unrewarding in many ways, and in my opinion still needs a lot of improvements. Right now it feels like you have to spend 500+ hours (at least that's what it feels like) just to finish gearing a single character.

Making Mythic Sparks easier to obtain was a fantastic change. It finally allowed players to work toward the best items at a reasonable pace instead of relying on a 100+ hour lottery just to see one drop. The Cube system itself is also a good idea overall, since it adds more depth to the game and gives each season more potential. But as I already mentioned, it still needs work.

Current Season:

I've never had so little fun playing a Diablo 4 season as I have with this one.

Who thought changing the Mythic item system was a good idea? It was actually in a pretty decent spot. Why do you always feel the need to change things that the community already considers good or at least acceptable?

Why on earth was it considered a good idea to throw Unique items into the Mythic pool and allow them to become Mythics?

The Barbarian alone doesn't have around 10 Mythic items anymore—it now has over 60.

And as if that wasn't bad enough, someone also thought it would be a brilliant idea to lock only one or two affixes while making the other two completely random.

Seriously, Blizzard... what an amazing system.

By the time you finally get the item you want, you'll probably be dead in real life.

Grinding is fine. It's part of an ARPG. But only up to a certain point. With this system, how long are people actually supposed to play? Why are you trying so hard to artificially extend the grind?

You've managed to create a system where players literally pay with their lifetime.

Instead of being rewarded after a reasonable amount of effort, you now have to grind for countless hours, only for the item to end up being complete garbage because two random affixes ruined it.

Congratulations.

You've officially shown that you've become exactly like EA and Ubisoft.

As long as the money keeps coming in, nothing else seems to matter. The community finally praises a feature and enjoys it? Great—better ruin it in the very next season.

Thanks for that.

And whoever came up with this Mythic item rework... maybe consider firing them. That would actually be a good decision for once.

Who doesn’t know what Diablo is? Blizzard, apparently, but as far as the players go, you usually know what to expect. Action RPG with top down view, dark fantasy setting, lots of enemies to kill, experience to get, loot to grab. After the simple but strong beginning with the first game, that is still my personal favorite, Diablo II established lots of canonical elements that are still used with little change across numerous games of numerous genres. While the often criticized (mostly for good reasons) third game made each playable class feel truly unique, something that is mostly continued with this newest game.

The different builds within each class can also be very different. Although, arguably, the choice is more limited than with the previous game. This has been done, seemingly, in the attempt to answer the criticism of the skill system of Diablo III, where you just unlocked new abilities and could switch them on the fly, thus removing any choice and commitment to how you build your characters. But in reality, the change is mostly in terms of presentation – while you have to commit to a build, you can also refund anything at any point (it just costs gold to do so). Nonetheless, the basic premise of the skills and how they fit into 6 specific slots remains exactly the same – I think it’s perfectly fine, but there might be people who prefer the classic freeform approach instead.

Some of the ideas from Diablo II that were either absent or limited in the previous game return as well, although often in a changed form. Time of day is yet again dynamic, something that was limited to post-campaign in the third game. Instead of the run and stamina from II we get a dodge move that works on a cooldown and in the later part of the campaign you unlock horses you can ride. The overall presentation is yet again more subdued and dark fantasy, after the extremely exciting and explosive epic adventuring of the third game. The music is made to be reminiscent of the classic soundtracks by Matt Uelmen and sound pretty good at times. The potions are yet again limited, but restock in towns or from the enemy drops and work as an ability, not an item. They actually feel closer to one of the variations that were attempted with Diablo III, before it was switched to just one infinite ability on a cooldown. And, frankly, I feel that this change back to a limited number is mostly pointless in practice.

Some things have been changed or removed. The hirelings/followers mechanic is now completely gone. You don’t lose experience or money upon death – instead the item durability serves as the “punishment” and items only ever lose durability to deaths now. Enchanting and crafting has been reworked a lot and an item upgrade mechanic has been introduced. All of the combo mechanics from the previous game are gone while the Paragon system has been reworked into something that is vaguely reminiscent of the License Board from Final Fantasy XII.

But the biggest and most destructive change to everything is in the way the world now works. Every Diablo game until now had completely random locations with specific key rooms or areas that these random roads connected to in-between. And the pace of a Diablo game has always been to move forward. You mowed down enemies, completed quests, explored all on the way to your next goal. Never backtracking, never getting lost even in the most confusing and open levels of Act III in Diablo II. It was a focused experience. Diablo IV is not. It’s structured like an open world game or an MMORPG. And it’s designed without any understanding of what makes a good open world game or a good Diablo game.

The world is huge, not random and full of constant and most tedious backtracking imaginable. But at the same time, enemies and events respawn almost immediately after you go far away from them. Dungeons? Random, extremely long, tedious, full of instantly recognizable boring randomized patterns and tasks that are always exactly same. There are over a hundred dungeons in the game and about a dozen possible task variations they require and, I think, less than 10 possible boss fights in them. Oh and if you complete a dungeon, then find a quest that sends you to this dungeon, the dungeon is reset again.

I’ve never ever played a Diablo game where I wasn’t killing everything in my way. Up until this one. In this one I was running away from enemies 80% of my time with it. Not because there was any difficulty with fighting them, but because it was boring. I couldn’t imagine in the 90s that I would ever play a Diablo game and upon finding a new group of enemies, my reaction would be “ugh”. But that’s what Diablo IV is. There’s no permanence or meaningfulness to anything you do in the world for you to want to engage with anything in this open world. There’s no reason to explore dungeons that you find, because they’re boring and you might need to do this boring thing again later if a quest requires it, so there’s no joy in discovery. Map opens in giant chunks to prevent any clear understanding of where you were and where you weren’t to find hidden collectibles. And all at the same time, the main Diablo gameplay loop feels tedious when there’s no clear line, when enemies are not in your way because there is no way, just open spaces to get bored in.

And it’s not like we don’t have good action RPGs with a similar structure, as even going back to the Diablo II days there was Divine Divinity or Sacred that had an open world structure and Diablo-like gameplay. But they knew better to use Ultima as example for the world and Diablo for the fun mechanics. While Diablo IV uses tedious grind of a generic MMO as an example for all that it brings.

And yes it is, yet again, always online. And it’s inexcusable and pointless as it was with Diablo III. Except now you can’t even have a private playthrough as the other players are always present in some way in “your” world and this whole MMO-like aspect is baked into the basics of the game. And it sucks.

To give the game some credit – even though the story isn’t particularly good, it is trying and sometimes it even has great moments and main story quests. The focus on the orthodox church teachings in contrast to the catholic church from the previous games isn’t as interesting as the developers seem to think, but I suppose for players from certain parts of the world it would at least feel novel. And it does look nice – this visual style is far closer to how one would’ve expected the first two Diablo games to be if they were fully 3D than what Diablo III attempted.

But it’s just so so horribly boring. And every single design decision that it has seems to be based on the desire to make things slow, to make things grindy. And no update or expansion or anything can fix what is, at its core, and extremely unfun game. I despise this game and cannot in good faith recommend anyone to play it. Play anything else instead, including Diablo III – at least it tried to be exciting and not miserable by design.

I have played every season of Diablo IV since launch. I am also an older gamer, which probably colors how I look at the game. I am not trying to race anyone, impress anyone, or turn every season into a second job. I want a good ARPG power fantasy, a reason to log in, a character that gets stronger in satisfying ways, and enough stuff to do that I can pick my own level of seriousness.

For me, Diablo IV has become one of the better games in a surprisingly thin ARPG landscape. I play Path of Exile 2 (913 hours) , Last Epoch (1,800 hours), Grim Dawn (612 hours) and Diablo IV (654 hours) .  Don't judge those times, I am retired and enjoy ARPGs! They all do different things well, but Diablo IV has its own lane. It is more approachable, more polished moment to moment, and much easier for me to just sit down, relax, kill demons, make numbers go up, and enjoy the fantasy of becoming absurdly powerful.

The game is much better now than it was at launch. The endgame has been fleshed out a lot. There are more systems layered on top of each other, more reasons to move around the world, more ways to work on a character, and more activities that feel like they feed into the larger loop instead of just being isolated chores. It still has that “log in, pick a thing, smash monsters, improve gear” rhythm, but now there are enough things to pick from that it feels more complete.

I also really like the open world. A lot of ARPGs are basically menus that teleport you into monster hallways. Diablo IV has towns, zones, strongholds, events, world bosses, Helltides, quest chains, dungeons, little side stories, and all the environmental flavor that makes Sanctuary feel like an actual place. The campaigns are high quality, the production values are excellent, and there are a surprising number of quests if you slow down enough to notice them.

That last part matters. Questing is best enjoyed with a very low-level character on Normal or Hard. Once your build is online and you are blowing up entire screens, the beautiful dungeons, terrain, monsters, and little details all become a stream of diluted pixels. That is fun too, obviously. That is the ARPG promise. But the game actually has a lot of atmosphere if you are not deleting the screen before your brain can process what you are looking at.

I enjoy both sides of the game. I like having permanent characters I can keep improving over time, but I also enjoy the disposable seasonal journey. That sounds negative, but I mean it positively. A season gives me an excuse to make a new character, play with the new systems, unlock cosmetics, check off the journey, and then move on when I am done. It does not always have to be a forever character. Sometimes it is just a fun seasonal project.

The cosmetics are also better than they get credit for. Yes, the cash shop is expensive. No argument there. But the seasonal Reliquary value is actually pretty good. If you count the platinum you get back from the Reliquary itself, it works out to roughly $7.50 a season for a pile of unlockable armor, weapons, mounts, pets, portals, and other cosmetics. Compared to the cash shop prices, that feels like the sane way to collect cool stuff. I like transmogs in general, and Diablo IV has a lot of great armor and weapon looks.

Crafting and gearing have also improved. It is still not perfect, and I am sure spreadsheet goblins can find ways to make anything complicated, but it is much easier to understand than it used to be. It has enough depth that improving a character feels meaningful, but it is not so opaque that I feel like I need to take a graduate course before replacing a pair of gloves. For the most part, I can understand what I am chasing, make progress toward it, and feel the character get stronger.

The community is another plus. Diablo IV has a good streaming and guide community, and that matters for this kind of game. You can play casually, but if you want to go deeper, there are people testing builds, explaining mechanics, pushing content, and doing the math. I like being able to bounce between “I am just chilling and killing monsters” and “okay, why exactly does this build work?”

Diablo IV is not a perfect ARPG, but I think it is very clearly a good one. It is chill, it looks great, it sounds great, the combat feels good, the power fantasy works, the endgame is much stronger than it used to be, and the seasonal structure gives me a reason to keep coming back without demanding that I live there.

For me, that is enough. More than enough, apparently, given the hours.

If you are a casual ARPG player, who
- just wants slay a variety of monsters for a few hours after work
- does not want to spend hours reading gudies and/or build a super-optimised character
- cares about above average music, sound direction and voice acting
- loves dark ambience and great graphics
- enjoys a more than decently written, well-acted campaign
- does not care that much about endgame and endless grinding after the campaign has ended
- thinks that 50 hours or so of fun is worth the price of the game
- does not expect a game to be fun after 1000+ hours
than I would recommend this game to you.

Despite my game hour investment, I can't give this installment into the Diablo series a positive review. Elements of the game work marvelously, most notably, the cinematics. Between the repetitive game play loop that doesn't really go anywhere and the grind for minimal rewards, the game loses its luster quickly.

The story is serviceable, but unfinished. Blizzard has opted for a continual story with limited resolutions to keep people paying for expansions. The main issue here is that quantity has taken priority over quality, which means you have loads of quests, most of which aren't memorable. In fact, you'll likely start skipping most of them. A few side quests do have their charms, but because the reward system is so banal, it's only worth it to get the progression bonuses. It is unlikely the lore will suck you as you'll feel mostly separate from it.

As for the progression system, it has its up and downs. You will go from feeling really powerful to utterly worthless if you switch to a different Torment too early. This wouldn't be so bad if the torment run you left weren't mind numbingly easy. And the drop rate is a bit absurd. While I appreciate a truly random feel to the drops, it does seem stacked against the player to try to challenge themselves. Most of the time, you can get better drops mass running easy mode than taking a risk against enemies that are challenging, but dropping the same garbage.

Then there are the instant kill mechanics, which I personally don't like. They're not used often enough to get the player to build up an understanding of them in general, but rather, just some single event situation to overcome and be done with it. I don't hold this against the developers entirely, but it does feel like a lazy way to make a game harder without doing much to the rest of the game to compensate for it. Sure, you can grind away the difficult bosses to learn their moves, but that grind only translates to those specific bosses. They don't really translate to anywhere else in the game. It can also make hardcore frustrating to all, but the most dedicated fans of the game.

Lastly: the shop. The shop is just plain bad. Not conceptually, in the sense of buying skins (but even that seems silly to me), but the overall cost per skin. Not only does Blizzard have a manipulative transaction scheme to get players to not think about the actual cost, the cost of each skin is priced in such away to pressure people into buying more so they don't "waste" left over platinum. Had they simply left it a straight currency cost and/or battle pass option, I'd be less bothered  by it. But the limited choices, the lack of a color wheel, and the manipulative pricing, it's just a regular slap in the face. And that's not even counting the regular slaps coming in the form of lazy Season design.

Bottom line: is it fun? Sure. I had a lot of fun, but it felt like empty fun. Not mindless fun. I have great mindless fun with Vampire Survivors, but empty fun. There's so much potential to Diablo 4 that was limited for unnecessary monetization options and focus on streamlined eye candy in lieu of a power fantasy with an interesting story. 

I think you'll have a better time in general with a different aRPG, unless you got a couple of friends who want to play. It's definitely more fun with other people, but even that is contingent on each individuals time investment potential.

Diablo IV has been a massive disappointment. I bought it with high hopes—despite the hefty price tag—and ended up feeling completely ripped off. After spending several hours with the game, I can confidently say: it’s not worth it, not even on sale.

The game is filled with meaningless level grinding that adds little to the experience. Each season forces you to start a new character from scratch, making all your previous progress feel pointless. The so-called “Eternal Realm” barely offers any content, and the seasonal updates don’t bring enough to justify the repetition.

They’ve stripped away the essence of what made Diablo special and replaced it with a generic online MMORPG shell, focused heavily on grind and monetization. Everything revolves around the in-game shop: skins, cosmetics, flashy armor sets… and yes, some of them cost €15–30 per bundle. You pay €60–100 for the game, only to find yourself in a glorified cosmetic storefront.

Even the inventory system has been dumbed down—gone is the iconic grid-based layout. Now it’s a bland, one-slot-per-item system like WoW, removing the unique strategy of managing space. And the loot? It used to be thrilling—legendary drops that truly changed your playstyle. Now it’s just uninspired stat boosts with no real impact.

In short: Diablo IV might look and run well, but it’s soulless, repetitive, and stripped of everything that once made Diablo great. It's built around seasonal FOMO and cosmetic sales instead of rewarding gameplay. It’s sad to see a beloved franchise reduced to this. I strongly do not recommend it.

I came into Diablo IV with a lot of skepticism.

Before playing it, I had already put more than 150 hours into Path of Exile 2 because I wanted to give that game a real chance. At the same time, I kept hearing how terrible Diablo supposedly was, how bad Blizzard was, how awful the launch had been, and so on.

And to be clear: Blizzard absolutely deserves criticism for some of the things the company has done in the past. I do not support that stuff.

But the developers, artists, designers, animators and everyone else actually working on Diablo are still people who clearly put a massive amount of work into this game.

And after finally buying Diablo IV on sale, I have to say something I genuinely did not expect:

**Diablo IV is one of the best games I have played in a long time.**

The biggest thing this game taught me is that I need to stop caring so much about online reviews.

Gaming discourse feels like one giant cycle of hype waves and hate waves. A game releases, everyone either calls it the greatest thing ever made or absolute garbage. At some point, you just have to play games yourself and decide whether you enjoy them.

And I am very glad I did.

For me, almost everything that frustrated me about Path of Exile is simply handled better in Diablo IV.

The first thing I love is the cosmetic and transmog system.

I can actually find cool-looking armor by simply playing the game. Some of the armor I have earned in-game genuinely looks better to me than things being sold for real money.

More importantly, I can change my appearance whenever I want. I can experiment, swap transmogs, change weapons and outfits without being charged five fucking euros every time I want to change the appearance of one item.

The paid cosmetics also feel much more reasonably priced to me than what I have experienced elsewhere.

That being said, the monetization is still one of my criticisms. Diablo is already a paid game with paid expansions, so having another premium cosmetic store on top does not feel great. I would really like some way to earn premium currency through gameplay, similar to Warframe or Guild Wars.

Then we get to what might be my favorite thing about Diablo IV:

**I can actually understand my own build.**

This sounds ridiculous until you have played Path of Exile.

In PoE, I can watch guide after guide and still feel like I understand nothing. There are layers upon layers of mechanics, currencies, affixes, systems and terminology. Sometimes it feels less like playing an ARPG and more like studying for an exam.

Diablo IV feels completely different.

I can create a character, decide that I want to play a Shadow Warlock, read what the abilities actually do, experiment with them and gradually create my own build.

And the crazy thing is:

**It actually works.**

I do not need a spreadsheet open on my second monitor. I do not need five browser tabs. I do not need someone with 8,000 hours explaining some obscure interaction the game never properly explains.

I read the skill.

I understand the skill.

I use the skill.

And the thing the description said would happen actually happens.

That is beautiful.

Diablo IV is one of the first ARPGs where I have genuinely enjoyed making my own builds without following a guide. I experimented, discovered interactions myself, realized when something was inefficient and slowly created a character that felt like mine.

The skill tree is simple enough to understand while still giving me meaningful decisions.

If I want Shadow damage, I can build around Shadow damage. If I want summons, I can build around summons. If I want to cast constantly, I can look for resource generation and abilities that support that playstyle.

My biggest criticism here is build diversity.

Path of Exile absolutely destroys Diablo when it comes to the sheer number of possibilities. Diablo offers different archetypes, but once you commit to a particular build, the gameplay can become repetitive.

That is the one area where I wish Diablo IV went much further.

If Blizzard kept this exact level of clarity and accessibility but gave every class two or three times as many abilities and interactions, the system would be incredible.

Because I do not want Diablo to become as complicated as Path of Exile.

I want Diablo's current system, just with more toys.

The loot is another massive win for me.

Something drops.

I pick it up.

I look at it.

I can immediately understand whether it might be useful.

Better damage. Better stats. Interesting effect. Cool legendary power.

Done.

I can actually be excited when something drops.

In Path of Exile, I sometimes get an item or currency drop and genuinely do not know whether I should be excited. Diablo's loot feels much cleaner. The drops feel relevant to my character, inventory management does not constantly feel like homework, and I spend more time killing monsters than trying to understand what entered my inventory.

The same applies to crafting and vendors.

I walk up to the blacksmith.

The game tells me what I can do.

I understand it.

I upgrade something, salvage something, craft something and move on.

The systems are intuitive without feeling meaningless. Gems make sense. Upgrading equipment makes sense. Salvaging makes sense. Changing aspects and improving gear makes sense.

The game actually teaches me how to use its systems instead of expecting me to watch a 45-minute YouTube video first.

And then there is the world itself.

This game scratches the fantasy RPG itch incredibly well.

I walk through Sanctuary, discover places, enter dungeons, find events, do side quests, get stronger, find better gear, unlock cosmetics and slowly turn my character into exactly the kind of fantasy character I wanted to play.

Sometimes I do not even need a larger objective. I can just put something on my second monitor, run around doing dungeons and side quests and enjoy killing things.

And the presentation is fantastic.

The story surprised me a lot.

I expected to mostly ignore it, but I actually became interested.

The cinematics are genuinely incredible and Lilith in particular is a fantastic villain. She has presence, looks incredible, feels dangerous and is not just presented as some generic demon screaming about destroying the world.

Her motivations are interesting enough that I actually wanted to understand what she was doing and why.

Overall, Diablo IV is basically the ARPG I wanted Path of Exile to be.

Path of Exile has far more complexity and significantly deeper build diversity, and I completely understand why some players prefer that.

But for me, complexity is not automatically depth.

Sometimes complexity is just complexity.

Diablo IV gives me enough systems to experiment with while still allowing me to understand what I am doing.

I can create my own build.

I can understand my gear.

I can understand crafting.

I can change things whenever I want.

I can find cool cosmetics by actually playing.

And most importantly:

**I spend my time playing the game instead of studying the game.**

That is why, for me, Diablo IV is comfortably better than Path of Exile.

It is not perfect.

The build variety could be much bigger and the monetization could be more player-friendly.

But the foundation is so damn good.

It is intuitive without being braindead and accessible without feeling completely shallow.

Sometimes I just want to enter a dungeon, find some sick armor, make my character stronger, experiment with a build I created myself and absolutely delete some demons.

Diablo IV lets me do exactly that.

And apparently I almost missed it because the internet told me the game sucked.

I am very glad I stopped listening.

Diablo IV: Premium Reskin Simulator

After two seasons (including current), it’s painfully clear what Diablo IV has become: a high-gloss storefront for paid cosmetics, sprinkled with a thin layer of recycled content and legacy critical bugs (main currency easy dupe). Here’s the honest breakdown of recent "seasonal updates":

95% — Brand new paid MTX: skins, mounts, emotes, and whatever else can be sold at a premium to distract from the gameplay void.
5% — Persistent bugs: gold dupes, consumable exploits, broken boss summoning—still haunting the servers two years.
5% — Old seasonal mechanics in slightly different outfits, renamed and repackaged as fresh content.

Calling this "seasonal content" is a stretch. Removing a shrine after two years? Changing the tint on Helltides? Reintroducing the same powers with different labels? Somehow, despite months of development time and the backing of a billion-dollar company, we’re left with glorified hotfixes and a battle pass featuring recolored assets no one can see half the time. Meanwhile, the core gameplay loop remains untouched, stale, and completely disconnected from the seasonal themes.

Entire seasons launch with game-breaking exploits still in place, and the economy is already broken by day one. Server-side dupes have become part of the Diablo identity.

Until then, we’ll be here. Waiting for the next “season” to drop with a recycled boss, a purple Helltide, and a $25 horse.

As a long-time player of Diablo, I had high expectations for Diablo IV from the very beginning. Honestly, at launch it was pretty rough – the game felt unfinished, a lot of expected features were missing, and overall it just didn’t hit the mark.

But I have to say, over time Diablo 4 is slowly starting to move closer to what made Diablo 3 fun. Some people might see that as a bad direction, but considering how the game started, I think it’s actually the right move. And so far, it’s showing.

If Season 13 delivers the way the trailers suggest, then Blizzard  might have actually cooked something good. The biggest thing is that we’re supposed to get a completely reworked skill tree, which could shake things up in a big way. If done right, it could bring a huge variety of new builds, more creativity, and finally give players the feeling that they can build their character their own way instead of just following one meta build online.

The only thing that still bothers me is the seasonal system. Every season brings a new mechanic, but it rarely stays for the next one. On one hand, that’s a shame because some of those ideas deserve to stay. On the other hand… maybe it’s actually a good thing. We could’ve ended up with another Path of Exile (and I say that as a fan), where there’s so much going on that new players just get confused and lost in all the systems.

That said, Season 13 is also bringing the Horadric Cube back, which is a big deal especially for crafting. It should allow for more efficient item manipulation and crafting options, while also bringing back some older seasonal crafting mechanics. If done right, this could be the perfect balance – keeping the good systems from the past without turning the game into a mess.

The Torment 12 is also supposed to return in Season 13, so I’m really curious to see how that turns out. This could finally be the kind of endgame activity the game has been missing – something that pushes you to test your builds, optimize them, and gives you a real reason to grind for better gear. It should also improve the overall endgame experience, because right now Torment 4 is honestly pretty easy – players can get there within 10–20 hours and end up one-shotting everything, which kind of kills the challenge.

Overall, it feels like the game is finally moving in the right direction. The gameplay is smoother, builds make more sense, loot feels more rewarding, and if the new skill system lives up to expectations, this could be a major turning point for the game.

I really wish the best for this game… just don’t mess it up.

BE WARNED:

System requirements are incorrect. The game requires about 320GB of free space.
As of August 1st, an updated copy of the game weighs in at about 158GB on my SSD. 
However, there's something wrong with the update process. Instead of updating the game, it creates a copy of the ENTIRE GAME, and then proceeds to update the copy. The copy is then placed on top of the previous version, replacing it.
This means that every time there's a 500MB update to the game, you will temporarily need enough free space for TWO FULL INSTALLS, or about 320GB. Not having enough space for this will just result in Diablo occupying your entire hard drive, probably causing other issues, and stalling the update with an "Insufficient disk space error" on steam. If you don't have enough free space to update the game, just go the roundabout way. Uninstal the game and re-install. This will download an already updated copy. This will take a few hours on a decent connection.
If you have limited data, then may Bobby Kotick have mercy on your soul, for you will have to re-download 160GB every time there's a minor update. 
Until this is fixed, I have no choice but to give this game a negative review.

I bought the first expansion on sale, and less then a few months after that they announce new expansion that includes the old one, and give 0 discount to anyone who bought the first expansion.

My main problem with Diablo 4 is not that there are paid expansions. I have absolutely no problem with paying for an expansion if it offers good content.

What I find highly questionable is the way Blizzard is handling things, and my criticism boils down to two simple points:

1. Forcing you to buy the DLC because otherwise the gameplay of characters YOU ALREADY PAID FOR is restricted.

2. Punishing players who supported the game from the beginning by making them pay more.

CRITICISM 1: NOT BUY DE DLC'S LIMITS THE GAMEPLAY OF CHARACTERS YOU ALREADY PAID FOR

What really bothers me is limiting the gameplay of characters I already purchased by locking content behind another expansion.

With Lord of Hatred, for example, there are options and specializations within the skill trees that can only be used if you own the DLC. And this directly affects characters that were already part of the game I purchased.

There is a huge difference between not buying an expansion and not being able to access certain areas or play certain classes.

And there is a completely different situation where the message is: if you don't buy the DLC, your existing character has skills or options that you simply cannot use.

The first one is completely reasonable to me. The second is a terrible practice, and I sincerely hope Blizzard reconsiders it.

If I bought the game and a class/character, I believe I should be able to enjoy its full gameplay within the content I purchased. Expansions should expand the experience, not start placing restrictions on characters and systems that were already part of the game.

And this is especially concerning because it essentially creates a paywall around gameplay. You are not simply paying for additional content; you are paying to unlock new possibilities for characters you already own.

CRITICISM 2: THE PRICE YOU MAKE PLAYERS WHO SUPPORTED YOU FROM THE BEGINNING PAY FOR A NEW DLC

The other point I find highly questionable is the way you treat the community that supported you from the beginning.

On top of buying the base game, I bought Vessel of Hatred when it was released for $40 USD. Now, with the release of Lord of Hatred, also at $40 USD, players who did not own Vessel of Hatred are getting that expansion for free as part of their purchase, while those of us who already bought it receive no meaningful discount or benefit toward the new DLC.

In other words, those of us who supported the game and bought the expansion from the beginning for $40 USD now have to pay another $40 USD for the new DLC, while someone who didn't buy the previous expansion essentially gets a 2-for-1 deal.

Seriously, Blizzard?

I think this is a terrible way to treat the players who supported the game from its early stages. So, as a response, I will not be buying future DLCs at launch either. I'll wait until you release another one for $40 USD and use it to give away all the previous ones. Until then, you won't get a single cent of my money.
